newsitem.title: USA: Swiss franc crumbles vs dollar, mark by US close.
newsitem.headline: Swiss franc crumbles vs dollar, mark by US close.

text.p: The dollar powered to its highest perch against the Swiss franc in 44 months and bounced back from a mid-session sell-off to reclaim its heady opening levels against the mark in U.S. trade on Thursday.

Encouraged by the sharp rise in dollar/Swiss, which has lagged the recent rise in dollar/mark, dealers said the greenback is starting to show considerable strength of its own and showing that it is not dependent on mark weakness for its gains.
"At the beginning of the year there was dollar buying, but now it's really starting to take hold," said John Hazelton, chief dealer at Manufacturers and Traders Bank.
"What I think we're seeing is the beginning of the realization that we are actually in a dollar move as opposed to a mark move."
The dollar hit a high of 1.51 Swiss francs -- its top level since November 1993 -- in afternoon trade and ended at 1.5053/63 francs, up over two centimes from its opening rate of 1.4850/55.
The dollar also held on to most of its gains against the mark after surging to a new six-year peak of 1.84 marks in European dealings.

After a heavy bout of dollar/mark profit-taking and short-covering in the mark crosses knocked the dollar back below 1.83 marks near mid-session, the greenback battled back to end at 1.8322/32 marks, down from 1.8350/55 at the open.

Remarks from Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing, who said in a television interview that he could not say he was not concerned about the speed and size of the mark's decline against the dollar, came late in the day and had little effect on the dollar/mark rate.
The Bundesbank's decision to stick with a fixed rate repo on Thursday was a sign to many that German officials are willing to live with a weak mark.

German central bank policymakers did leave the door open for a change to a variable rate repo during their upcoming month-long recess, taking the unusual step of setting their fixed rate tender for only two weeks.
But most experts saw the move as more of a tactical message for the market and downplayed the possibility of inter-meeting action on the rate.

"The Bundesbank complaints about the strong dollar have been rather half-hearted so far," said Chris Iggo, chief economist at BZW Securities. "They just want to keep the powder dry in case this whole thing gets out of control."
Even more impressive than the move in dollar/mark on Thursday was the slide in the Swiss franc against both the dollar and the mark, dealers said.

Heavy sales of Swiss francs for marks by U.S. funds and banks pushed the mark/Swiss rate up to 0.8215 from a low of 0.8090. Even as it shrank against the dollar, the mark also staged a nice rally on other European crosses.

"We saw some unwinding of a lot of the short-mark crosses that have been in place," said John McCarthy, senior vice president at ING Barings Capital Markets. "Mark/swiss is up a full centime on the day which is an extraordinary move."
In other trade on Thursday, the dollar benefitted from its gains against Europe and pushed up to close at 116.05/15 yen versus 115.58/68 at the open.
Sterling edged down to $1.6750/60 from an opening rate of $1.6760/70 and the Australian dollar recovered to $0.7360/65 from $0.7350/60.
The dollar edged up marginally to Canadian $1.3815/20 from C$1.3813/18.
